replying_to: Replying to A Two-Stage Data-Free Adversarial Patch Generation Framework
display_title: Official Review of Paper2263 by Reviewer gFPs

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper mainly studies the generation of adversarial patch in data-free scenarios with higher requirements on data privacy. In this two-stage framework, it first uses proxy dataset selection (PDS) method to calculate the average patch saliency (APS) of each available dataset, and then used patch generation (PG) method which applies the designed data-free Expectation over Transformation (DFEoT) based on the determined proxy dataset for patch generation.
content.main_review:
Pros: 
1. From the perspective of significance, it is meaningful to study data-free scenarios of this paper, because deep learning models in real life often set a high protection level for data privacy in actual deployment.
2. From the perspective of technical details, it is reasonable and intuitive to split the patch generation in the data-free scenario into the selection of the proxy data set and the subsequent patch generation.
3. As for the calculation and application of patch saliency metric and its average version, the overall theoretical derivation is relatively rigorous. In addition, the author also considers the sensitivity of the initial value when the patch is generated, and the overall logic is relatively complete.

After reading the paper I have some concerns as follow:
1. The important value of the adversarial patch is its effectiveness on attacks in the physical environment. Although the calculation method in this paper is based on EOT, I think it is still necessary to verify the validity of the generated patches in real physical environment.
2. Although the two-stage design is intuitive, is there some strong coupling between the selection of data sets and the generation of patches? If so, will the phased optimization not give full play to the interaction between the two factors to some extent? Of course, this is just my thinking. If there was a way to optimize both simultaneously rather than sequentially, would the attack result be better?
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, this paper is meaningful. But the concerns should be addressed.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.

content.title: Response to Official Review of Paper2263 by Reviewer gFPs
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your positive review! Your comments are very enlightening and instructive for our future work. The reviewer comments are laid out below in italicized font and specific concerns have been numbered. Our response and changes/additions to the manuscript are given in normal font.

***Q1: "The important value of the adversarial patch is its effectiveness on attacks in the physical environment. Although the calculation method in this paper is based on EOT, I think it is still necessary to verify the validity of the generated patches in the real physical environment."***

A1: We totally understand your concern. We agree the real-world test is important. The current work mainly explores digital attacks in data-free scenarios and the model‘s ability to protect the privacy of training data. An experimental platform for physical environment testing is currently under construction. Our future work is mainly to consider how to obtain robust attack results in the presence of relative motion between the camera and the patch based on the current work.  

***Q2: "Although the two-stage design is intuitive, is there some strong coupling between the selection of data sets and the generation of patches? If so, will the phased optimization not give full play to the interaction between the two factors to some extent? Of course, this is just my thinking. If there was a way to optimize both simultaneously rather than sequentially, would the attack result be better?"***

A2: Thanks for your enlightening comment! We have indeed considered this issue, and there is actually a little contradiction in it. From the perspective of attack results, we do not deny that simultaneous optimization may bring better attacks than sequential optimization given the fact a successful simultaneous optimization example has already existed in the adversarial training [1]. From the perspective of compatibility, we expect that the selection of the proxy dataset and the generation of patches can be relatively independent. We think it may help the general patch generation methods (using training data) be directly applied to data-free scenarios.

Overall, research on data-free attacks is still relatively rare compared to its importance and this work is our preliminary exploration of attacks in data-free scenarios. We will carefully consider how to achieve simultaneous optimization while ensuring compatibility in future work.


Thanks for your comments again! We would be glad to respond to any further questions and comments that you may have.

[1] Aleksander Madry, Aleksandar Makelov, Ludwig Schmidt, Dimitris Tsipras, and Adrian Vladu.Towards deep learning models resistant to adversarial attacks.arXiv preprint arXiv:1706.06083,2017.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2263 by Reviewer 58cw

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on generating adversarial patches under the data-free scenario. Specifically, this paper proposes a two-stage pipeline: (1) select proxy dataset using patch saliency as a metric; (2) a novel adversarial patch generation method which not only updates the patch but also updates the image background during the generation procedure. The experiments show that the proposed method achieves better results than the baseline method.
content.main_review:
The strengths: 

(1) the proposed method looks reasonable to me, so the results are reasonably good.

(2) the problem, data-free adversarial patch generation, is interesting

The weaknesses:

(1) The main concern is the paper writing issues. I spent a lot of time understanding this paper but still cannot guarantee my understanding is correct. I think one of the difficulties to understand this paper is because there are too many rare abbreviations, such as APG, APS, EoT, DF-EoT, TFR, UFR, PDS,  PG, etc. Although the readers could go back to find the definition of them, these abbreviations still make it difficult to read this paper smoothly.

(2) Although the performance improved according to Table 2, it is still not clear if the proposed method leads to a larger computational cost -- it seems the proposed method is more complex than the baseline method.

(3) If my understanding is correct, Section 3.3 is evaluating the proxy dataset selection stage while Section 3.4 is evaluating the adversarial patch generation stage. However, I don't find the final performance comparison between the baseline method and the full version of the proposed method (ie, proxy selection stage + patch generation stage)
content.summary_of_the_review: I like the topic of this paper. However, due to the weakness mentioned above, I think this paper is still improvable before publishing. Specifically, the writing does not meet the ICLR bar.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.details_of_ethics_concerns: I am not sure if Section 5 Acknowledge is appropriate during the peer-review stage.
content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.

content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for the precious feedback. We believe you have a quite good understanding of our work based on your comments. The reviewer comments are laid out below in italicized font and specific concerns have been numbered. Our response and changes/additions to the manuscript are given in normal font. We would be glad to respond to any further questions and comments that you may have. 


***"Q1: The proposed method looks reasonable to me, so the results are reasonably good. "***

A1: We are thankful for your positive evaluation! To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work focusing on adversarial patch generation in data-free scenarios. The proposed proxy dataset selection metric enables the benchmark patch generation method (i.e., EoT) can be directly applied to data-free scenarios. The proposed patch generation method humanely considers the attacker‘s ability to collect data and improves patch fooling ability on artificially synthesized datasets (e.g., uniform random noise) compared with EoT.


***"Q2:The problem, data-free adversarial patch generation, is interesting."***

A2: Thank you for your positive review！As the other reviewer mentioned, deep learning models in real life often set a high protection level for data privacy in actual deployment. Our research also reflects the models' protection level of data privacy. After all, in most cases, the proposed proxy dataset selection metric successfully identify the training dataset from the available datasets in this work.


***Q3:“The main concern is the paper writing issues. I spent a lot of time understanding this paper but still cannot guarantee my understanding is correct. I think one of the difficulties to understand this paper is because there are too many rare abbreviations, such as APG, APS, EoT, DF-EoT, TFR, UFR, PDS, PG, etc. Although the readers could go back to find the definition of them, these abbreviations still make it difficult to read this paper smoothly.”***

A3: Thanks for taking your valuable time to read this paper. We have tried our best to polish the revised paper in response to your comment. A list of the abbreviations has been attached to“Appendix B” (page 12).

***Q4:“ Although the performance improved according to Table 2, it is still not clear if the proposed method leads to a larger computational cost -- it seems the proposed method is more complex than the baseline method.”***

A4: This is a very insightful comment based on the sharp observation that DF-EoT is more computationally expensive than EoT due to the complexity. 
> The average time of generating a patch using DF-EoT on GPU RTX 2080 is approximately 90 seconds. In the same condition, EoT takes about 38 seconds. Nonetheless, the computational cost is acceptable considering the DF-EoT's improved performance in data-free scenarios.

The above clarification has been added in the third paragraph section “3.1 Experimental Setting” (page 7).

Q5:“ If my understanding is correct, Section 3.3 is evaluating the proxy dataset selection stage while Section 3.4 is evaluating the adversarial patch generation stage. However, I don‘t find the final performance comparison between the baseline method and the full version of the proposed method (ie, proxy selection stage + patch generation stage).”

A5: Thank you very much for this comment, and your understanding is correct. A table for the comparison between EoT using the training data and DF-EoT using the selected proxy dataset is as follows. 

>| Method  |                     VGG-16 |       VGG-19 |      ResNet-18 |   ResNet-34 |      Inception-V1|
| ----------- |                   ----------- |    ----------- |      ----------- |     ----------- |              ----------- |
| EoT                            | 96.65%    |        91.26%|      77.30%|       71.51%|                     60.71%|
| TS-DF Framework    | 96.47%     |       92.26%|       76.87%|       72.64%|                     80.71%|  

As we can see, the proposed two-stage data-free framework (TS-DF Framework) achieves comparable performance in data-free scenarios with the EoT using the training data. The above clarification has been added in “Appendix G” of the revised paper (page 14).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work aims to design a patch generation strategy for image attacks which place the patch on the original image to fool the well-trained image classifier, and the patch generation process has no access to the dataset used to train image classifier. To solve the data-free problem, this work advances the existing method EoT [1] with two additional steps. One is to select the proxy dataset with high average patch saliency. Another is to conduct multiple-time patch update.
content.main_review:
This work aims to design a patch generation strategy for image attacks which place the patch on the original image to fool the well-trained image classifier, and the patch generation process has no access to the dataset used to train image classifier. To solve the data-free problem, this work advances the existing method EoT [1] with two additional steps. One is to select the proxy dataset with high average patch saliency. Another is to conduct multiple-time patch update.

However, I still have several concerns about the current version:
1. There are so many abbreviations of the definitions. It is difficult for readers to directly get the point. It would be better to list these abbreviations in one Table for reference. Moreover, there are some minor grammatical errors to be revised.
2. In the main content, this paper does not explicitly formulate the data-free adversarial patch generation problem. And I am confused about the definition of symbols such as “an input image $X \in R^{d}$”. From the experiments, the image should be $X \in R^{C\times H\times W}$.
3. For the method, I am not clear why the selected dataset with the defined average patch saliency can guarantee patches’ fooling abilities for the unseen training dataset, and how to train the integrated gradient function in the patch saliency calculation. In addition, when comparing with EoT [1], updating the patch with multiple times is not significant difference.
4.	For the experiment, the current version only compares it with EoT [1]. It is difficult to reflect the effectiveness of the proposed method. It would be better to compare it with more baselines.

[1] Anish Athalye, Logan Engstrom, Andrew Ilyas, and Kevin Kwok. Synthesizing robust adversarial examples. In International conference on machine learning (ICML), 2018.
content.summary_of_the_review: There are some unclear parts in the current version (See the main review).

content.title: Response To Official Review of Paper 2263  by Reviewer tTEH (1/2)
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for the valuable feedback. Your comments are very constructive and have helped us improve the quality of our manuscript. The reviewer comments are laid out below in italicized font and specific concerns have been numbered. Our response and changes/additions to the manuscript are given in normal font. 

***Q1: "There are so many abbreviations of the definitions. It is difficult for readers to directly get the point. It would be better to list these abbreviations in one Table for reference. Moreover, there are some minor grammatical errors to be revised."***

A1: Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We have modified the manuscript in response to your comment. A list of the abbreviations has been attached to the “Appendix B” of our revised paper (page 12). 

***Q2.1: “ In the main content, this paper does not explicitly formulate the data-free adversarial patch generation problem.”***

A2.1: Thank you very much for this suggestion. The formulation of the data-free patch generation problem is as follow:

>Specifically, given attackers' available datasets {$\cal D_1, D_2\,...$}, the proposed two-stage data-free APG framework formalises the patch generation problem in data-free scenarios as the following equation: 
$$
P^{*} = arg \min\_{P} \mathbb{E}\_{X\sim \mathcal{D}\_{proxy},L\sim\mathcal{L},T \sim \mathcal{T}}  \mathcal{O}(\mathcal{F}(X_P),y'),
$$ where
$$
\mathcal{D}\_{proxy}=\mathcal{S}\_{PDS}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{F})
$$ 
and $\mathcal{S}\_{PDS}$ is a PDS metric reflecting APG methods' performance on $\mathcal{D}$.

The corresponding clarification has been added in the first paragraph of section "2.3 Two-Stage Data-Free APG Framework" of the revised paper (see page 4).

***Q2.2: "And I am confused about the definition of symbols such as “an input image X∈Rd”. From the experiments, the image should be X∈RC×H×W.”***


A2.2: Thank you for this comment to improve the rigour of our article. 
> We define an input image as ”$X\in \mathbb{R}\^{d}$” instead of “$X\in\mathbb{R}\^{C \times H \times W}$” for the simplicity of subsequent mathematical expression. 

And we have added the corresponding clarification where the definition first appears  (see the footnote on page 3).

***Q3.1: “ For the method, I am not clear why the selected dataset with the defined average patch saliency can guarantee patches’ fooling abilities for the unseen training dataset."***

A3.1: This is a very constructive comment that helps us to provide a more in-depth view of the proposed APS metric.
> Actually, the reason is that the access to the target model in the average patch saliency (APS) calculation process guarantees the patches’ fooling abilities. To put it in other words, APS ranks the available dataset by comparing the saliency of models’ extracted information. On the one hand, since the target model is trained on the training dataset, it can memorize features of its seen training data. The adversarial patch generation process can be seen as extracting such memorized information and mimicking these features, which explains why EoT using uniform random noise can achieve a certain degree of patch fooling ability in Table 1. On the other hand, the saliency of extracted features varies with the selected proxy dataset. The closer the features in the proxy data are to the memorized features, the greater the patch saliency (PS), which explains why the original training dataset is assigned the highest APS value and uniform random noise is assigned the lowest value in Table 1. Therefore, by comparing the average PS of generated patches on each dataset, APS can serve as a proxy dataset selection metric and guarantee patches’ fooling abilities on the unseen training dataset.

The above clarification has been added at the end of section ”3.3.2 Consistency between APS and ATFR” of the revised paper (see page 8).

***Q3.2: “ how to train the integrated gradient function in the patch saliency calculation ?”***

A3.2: Thanks for this comment. The integrated gradient function does not involve a training process. Specifically
>Integrated Gradient is a technique for visualising pixel importance (i.e., saliency) in the field of explainable machine learning. Given an image-label pair $(X,y)$ and a classifier $\mathcal{F}$,  the integrated gradient function $\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{F}}$ output a saliency map by the following equation:
$$
\mathcal{G}\_{\mathcal{F}}(X,y) = (X-X\_{\mathcal{G}})\times \int\_{\alpha =0}\^{1}\frac{\partial [\mathcal{F}(X\_{\mathcal{G}}+\alpha(X-X\_{\mathcal{G}}))]\_{y}}{\partial \alpha},\     (13)       
$$
where $X\_{\mathcal{G}}$ is a black image. Equation (13) is actually a path integral along the line segment between points $X\_{\mathcal{G}}$ and $X$, and the saliency map is the importance of each component in $X$ to the class $y$ with respect to $\mathcal{F}$.

The corresponding clarification has been added in the “Appendix C”(see page 12).

content.title: Response To Official Review of Paper 2263 by Reviewer tTEH (2/2)
content.comment:
***Q3.3: “when comparing with EoT, updating the patch multiple times is not significantly different.”***
 
A3.3: Thank you for the comment which helps us further clarify the proposed patch generation method. Data-free Expectation over Transformation (DF-EoT) is different from EoT in terms of **method** and **performance**.

For the **method**,
> compared with EoT, DF-EoT considers the update of sampled image backgrounds and patch initial value sensitivity. Specifically, DF-EoT differs from EoT in the following steps: i) background update, ii) multiple-time patch update and iii) restart selection steps.

Actually, updating the patch multiple times is only one of the steps of DF-EoT. The above clarification has been added in the first paragraph of section ”2.3.2 Stage II: Patch Generation”(page 6).

For the **performance** improvement compared with EoT,
>  DF-EoT increases patches' fooling abilities on a wide range of proxy datasets than EoT. For instance, DF-EoT improves ATFR to 78.34% by 35.63% for a low-APS dataset UNIFORM on the target model VGG-19 and increases ATFR to 84.33% by 21.76% for a high-APS dataset MSCOCO on the target model Inception-v1. 

The above clarification has been highlighted in the section “3.4.1 Improved Patch Fooling Ability via DF-EoT” (page 9).

***Q4: “ For the experiment, the current version only compares it with EoT [1]. It is difficult to reflect the effectiveness of the proposed method. It would be better to compare it with more baselines.”***

A4: Thank you very much for this comment! It provides us with a valuable opportunity to rethink and clarify our experiments in our revised paper. We hope the effectiveness of the proposed two-stage data-free patch generation framework can be supported by our **experimental design and results**. 

> For the **experimental design** of the **APS** evaluation, **1)** the  APS proposed in data-free scenarios is compared with a PDS metric computed with the original training data, average targeted fooling rates (ATFR). **2)** For the target models, we consider five different model architectures widely deployed in the industry. **3)** For the datasets, three large-scale datasets are included in the considered available datasets. Two manually synthesized datasets are also involved considering some attackers' limited data collection ability. For the **experimental results**, **1)** APS shows a high consistency with ATFR and successfully identifies the training dataset from available datasets in most cases (80%). **2)** A case-level consistency between APS and ATFR is also established. The mean consistency rate between patch saliency (PS) and targeted fooling rate (TFR) reaches 91% on all considered datasets.  

>For the **experimental design**, we admit that comparing with more baselines is better, but we also think comparing **DF-EoT** with EoT is sufficient. **1)** EoT is representative and reliable given the fact that it can even be used to synthesize 3-D adversarial objects. **2)**  To the best of our knowledge, DF-EoT is the first APG method targeted for data-free scenarios, while recent methods do not restrict access to the training dataset. **3)** We did not claim a SOTA performance on the general patch generation problem, as the name of DF-EoT suggests, we focus on data-free scenarios. For the **experimental results**, the performance improvement of DF-EoT compared to EoT is significant. **1)** DF-EoT improves the patch fooling ability on a wide range of proxy datasets (mentioned in A3.3). **2)** The consistency (91%) built between PS and TFR shows that DF-EoT can reliably alleviate the patch initial value sensitivity problem in data-free scenarios.

The above clarification has been added at 1) the last paragraph of section “2.2 The Benchmark APG Method: EoT”(page 3);  2) the second paragraph of section “3.1 Experimental Setting”(page 6); 3) the first paragraph of section “3.3.1 Consistency between APS and ATFR”(page 7);  4) section “3.4.1 Improved ATFR Patch Fooling Ability via DF-EoT” (page 9).


Your comment is very constructive and insightful! We would be glad to respond to any further questions and comments that you may have.
